When PADT (highest day of traffic projected for the year) is used, the peak one- and eight-hour traffic volumes for this day are an appropriate basis for calculating the one- and eight-hour carbon monoxide maximums. However, when AADT is used, the one- and eight-hour traffic maximums must be derived from factors designed to give the highest single hour and highest consecutive eight hours of traffic for the year from the AADT.
Although annual traffic peaks occurring any time during the year are an acceptable basis for demonstrating the approvability of a project, traffic peaks which happen to occur during the warm summer months are not the most appropriate traffic volumes to use in applying the EPA screening technique contained in Guidelines For Air Quality Maintenance Planning and Analysis, Volume 9: Evaluating Indirect Sources. Colder temperatures and shorter days tend to increase motor vehicle emissions and produce meteorological conditions less favorable for pollutant dispersion during the winter months. As a result of a telephone conversation with Dr. Edwin L. Meyer, one of the developers of the EPA screening technique, it was decided that traffic peaks occurring during the months of November through April would be appropriate to use in calculating the impact of highway projects on ambient carbon monoxide concentrations. This period covers the months during which carbon monoxide concentrations above the eight-hour standard were measured at more than one monitoring station in Milwaukee during the last two winters. Our approval of the Airport Spur was based on traffic projected for this period.
It should be pointed out that the truck mixes given in figures 19A, 19B, and 19C and accompanying text were not applied in the microscale analysis. The EPA curves used for this analysis are based on a national average mix of vehicles with about 88% light duty vehicles and 12% light duty trucks. In addition, the wind direction was assumed to be at an angle of 10° with the traffic lanes affecting the receptor and a wind speed of one meter per second and atmospheric stability D were assumed. These underlying assumptions should be mentioned when the Volume 9 screening method is used. The meteorological conditions included in the above assumptions were agreed upon as an acceptable worst-case basis for evaluating highway projects. The "worst probable" conditions with atmospheric stability F, as mentioned on pages 50 through 52, were not used in the microscale analysis reported in the October, 1975 Air Quality Report.
During the microscale analysis, a question arose as to how best to apply the EPA screening technique to a freeway interchange. Since the technique assumes that the wind makes an angle of 10° with all lanes of traffic, it is most accurately applied to parallel traffic lanes.
